name: Freund-Rubin Compactification
description: Anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions times a 7-sphere of twice its radius, a solution of supergravity in eleven dimensions. A field with four indices fills the four large dimensions evenly, and Peter Freund and Mark Rubin found in 1980 that it splits the eleven into four and seven of its own accord. In 1997 Juan Maldacena found it again as the throat of a stack of membranes.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: At the Enrico Fermi Institute in Chicago, in July 1980, Peter G. O. Freund and Mark A. Rubin went looking for a reason that a world of many dimensions would show us only four [freund1980]. Theories built on the old idea of Theodor Kaluza account for the forces and the matter of four dimensions with a simpler geometry in more, and they assume that the extra dimensions curl up to a tiny size [freund1980, kaluza1921]. Until then the curling had been done by fields added to the theory for that purpose, and Freund and Rubin called such additions "contrary to the spirit of unification" [freund1980, cremmer1976]. Their remark was that supergravity in more dimensions already carries fields other than gravity, and that those fields can do the curling themselves [freund1980].¶Their first example is Maxwell's field, pointing across two of the dimensions and nowhere else, the way an electric field points across the gap between two charged plates [freund1980]. Spacetime then splits into a surface and the rest, curved with opposite signs, and when the surface holds the time the rest closes up into a compact space [freund1980]. In four dimensions the two pieces come out equally curved, which is the universe of Bruno Bertotti and Ivor Robinson, anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a sphere of the same radius [freund1980, bertotti1959, robinson1959]. A field with $s$ indices does the same to $s$ dimensions, splitting $d$ dimensions into $s$ and $d - s$ [freund1980]. Supergravity in eleven dimensions has such a field with $s = 4$, so either seven of its ten space dimensions curl up or four do [freund1980]. If seven do, the large world has one time and three space dimensions, "a pleasing result" [freund1980].¶The eleven dimensions of that solution are anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions times a sphere of seven, $$ds^2 = -\cosh^2\!\rho\,c^2dt^2 + L^2\left(d\rho^2 + \sinh^2\!\rho\,d\Omega_2^2\right) + 4L^2d\Omega_7^2,$$ with $L$ the radius of anti-de Sitter space, $\rho$ the distance from its centre in units of $L$, and $d\Omega_2^2$ and $d\Omega_7^2$ the unit spheres of two and seven dimensions [freund1980, aharony2000, maldacena1998]. The field points along all four large dimensions at once, with the same strength everywhere, and it bends them into anti-de Sitter space, curved like a saddle, and the seven others into a sphere [freund1980, gibbons1993]. Each small dimension is curved half as much as each large one and with the opposite sign, which makes the radius of the sphere twice the radius of anti-de Sitter space [freund1980, maldacena1998]. On dimensional grounds the sphere is about a Planck length across, and then the large world has a cosmological constant of the opposite sign and of the same Planck size [freund1980]. "This is immense, so how does it get removed?" Freund and Rubin asked [freund1980].¶The round 7-sphere keeps all the supersymmetry of the theory, and the world of four dimensions inherits eight supersymmetries and, from the rotations of the sphere, the gauge group SO(8) [awada1983, gibbons1993]. Moustafa A. Awada, Michael J. Duff, and Christopher N. Pope squashed the sphere, its metric "distorted" so that its symmetry falls to SO(5) times SU(2) and the eight supersymmetries fall to one [awada1983, nilsson1984]. Bengt E. W. Nilsson and Pope described the round sphere as a bundle of circles over the complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^3$, and they showed that a known solution of supergravity in ten dimensions on $\mathbb{CP}^3$ is, in their words, "nothing more than the round seven-sphere solution in disguise" [nilsson1984]. When the field fills four dimensions of space, the same theory gives anti-de Sitter space of seven dimensions times a 4-sphere, a case worked out by Krzysztof Pilch, Peter van Nieuwenhuizen, and Paul K. Townsend under the title "11 = 7 + 4, too" [pilch1984]. None of these looked like our world, and Nilsson and Pope found that all of them "seem to suffer from severe difficulties", notably "the cosmological constant of order unity in Planck units, and the lack of a chiral fermion spectrum" [nilsson1984].¶Could ten dimensions do the same? They have a supergravity of their own, the chiral theory of type IIB, which no curling up of eleven can give and whose field strength with five indices is equal to its own dual [schwarz1983, gunaydin1985]. Its field equations came from John H. Schwarz in 1983, and with them a solution "easy to discover (found in discussions with N. Warner)" [schwarz1983]. The field is set along five dimensions, and since it equals its own dual it lies along the other five as well [schwarz1983]. Spacetime then splits into a space of five dimensions with negative curvature and one with positive curvature, "analogous to the 4 + 7 decomposition" of eleven, and with a round sphere the two are anti-de Sitter space and a 5-sphere of one radius [schwarz1983, maldacena1998, kim1985]. Harmonic analysis on that sphere gave H. J. Kim, Larry J. Romans, and Peter van Nieuwenhuizen "the complete mass spectrum" of its fields, and Murat Günaydin and Neil Marcus showed that its modes fall into unitary representations of $U(2,2/4)$, the supergroup of the geometry [kim1985, gunaydin1985].¶Seventeen years after Chicago the three geometries turned up again, each at the bottom of the throat of a stack of branes: the membrane of eleven dimensions, its fivebrane, and the three-brane of ten [gibbons1993, maldacena1998]. Juan Maldacena took the limit in which the field theory living on the branes comes apart from the gravity around them, which keeps the throat alone [maldacena1998]. His conjecture is that "compactifications of M/string theory on various Anti-deSitter spacetimes is dual to various conformal field theories" [maldacena1998]. For $N$ membranes the throat is Freund and Rubin's geometry, with the radius of the sphere fixed by $N$ and still twice the radius of anti-de Sitter space, and its partner is a conformal field theory of three dimensions [maldacena1998]. Günaydin and Marcus's supergroup $U(2,2/4)$ is also the superconformal group of the gauge theory in four dimensions, so the geometry and the gauge theory share one supersymmetry [maldacena1998, gunaydin1985].

related.text: The four large dimensions. Every point of anti-de Sitter space carries a 7-sphere of twice its radius [freund1980, maldacena1998].
The sister in ten dimensions. Its throat is anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions times a 5-sphere, and there the two radii are equal [schwarz1983, maldacena1998].

Freund and Rubin's own first case, Maxwell's field pointing across two dimensions of four, comes out as this universe: anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions times a sphere of the same radius [freund1980, bertotti1959].

Extra dimensions curled up by a monopole put in for the purpose. Freund and Rubin used a field that supergravity carries already, and called such additions "contrary to the spirit of unification" [cremmer1976, freund1980].

Kaluza and Klein's circle twisted over a sphere, which at each radius makes a 3-sphere [grossperry1983, nilsson1984]. Nilsson and Pope described the round 7-sphere the same way, as circles twisted over the complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^3$ [nilsson1984].
A black hole in anti-de Sitter space. In Maldacena's correspondence a black hole in the throat of the membranes is their field theory at a finite temperature [maldacena1998].

A charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space. Andrew Chamblin, Roberto Emparan, Clifford V. Johnson, and Robert C. Myers found such holes in gauged supergravity, which in four dimensions comes from the round 7-sphere, with the charge coming from a rotation in the directions of the sphere [chamblin1999, awada1983].
Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum's "alternative to compactification": a fifth dimension of infinite size, curved so that gravity on a three-brane looks like gravity in four dimensions [randall1999b].
Another product of a spacetime of two dimensions and a sphere: de Sitter space times a sphere of the same radius, held by a positive cosmological constant [nariai1950].

coordinates.name: Global

parameters.description: Radius of anti-de Sitter space, a length; the 7-sphere has the radius $2L$, and the field strength with four indices is $f\,\epsilon$, with $\epsilon$ the volume form of the anti-de Sitter factor and $8\pi Gf^2 = 3/4L^2$, where $G$ is the gravitational constant of eleven dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi, \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \kappa, \xi, \omega, \psi)$, with $t$ a time and $\rho$ a pure number that measures the distance from the centre of anti-de Sitter space in units of $L$. The angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ are those of its spheres, and $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\kappa$, $\xi$, $\omega$, and $\psi$ those of the 7-sphere. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi, \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \kappa, \xi, \omega, \psi)$, with $t$ a time and $\chi$ the angle with $\tan\chi = \sinh\rho$ of the global chart, so that the boundary of anti-de Sitter space is at $\chi = \pi/2$. The angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ are those of its spheres, and $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\kappa$, $\xi$, $\omega$, and $\psi$ those of the 7-sphere.
